<div class="quiz">
<div class="quiz-title">Q1: A strong correlation</div>
<p class="quiz-question">You have four small data sets, each with an <code>x</code> and a <code>y</code> variable. In all four, the correlation between <code>x</code> and <code>y</code> is exactly the same: <em>r</em> = 0.82, <em>p</em> &lt; .01. A colleague concludes that the relation between <code>x</code> and <code>y</code> is the same in all four data sets, so there is no need to plot them. Why is it still a good idea to plot them?</p>
<ul class="quiz-choices">
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="true" data-explain="Right — this is exactly what Anscombe's quartet shows: four data sets with identical correlations, where one is a normal linear relation, one is curved, and two are driven by a single outlier. The correlation summarizes the data in a single number; only a plot shows whether that number tells the right story.">The same correlation can come from very different patterns, such as a curved relation or a single outlier.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — a plot doesn't test significance; the correlation test already told you that (p &lt; .01). What a plot adds is the shape of the relation, which can be very different even when the correlation is identical.">A plot can show whether the correlation is really significant.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — a correlation is computed exactly from the data, so it is not imprecise. The problem is that a single number can hide very different patterns, such as a curve or an outlier, which you only see when you plot the data.">A plot gives a more precise estimate of the strength of the relation than <em>r</em>.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — plotting is useful for strong correlations too. In Anscombe's quartet, all four correlations are strong and significant, but two of them are caused by a single outlier.">It isn't: plotting is only needed when the correlation is weak or not significant.</li>
</ul>
<p class="quiz-feedback" hidden></p>
</div>

<div class="quiz">
<div class="quiz-title">Q2: Colored points, black names</div>
<p class="quiz-question">The data frame <code>gap_sample</code> contains these five countries from 2010:</p>

| country | continent | infant_mortality | fertility |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Nigeria | Africa | 81.5 | 6.02 |
| Brazil | Americas | 14.8 | 1.84 |
| India | Asia | 46.3 | 2.56 |
| Germany | Europe | 3.5 | 1.39 |
| Australia | Oceania | 4.1 | 1.89 |

<p>You want a scatter plot where the points are colored by continent, and each point is labeled with the name of the country in black text (<code>geom_text</code> draws a text for each row, using the <code>label</code> aesthetic). Which code does that?</p>
<ul class="quiz-choices">
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="true" data-explain="Right — a mapping inside a geom only applies to that geom. So only the points are colored by continent, while geom_text uses its default black color. The x and y mappings in the ggplot() call are shared by both layers."><code>ggplot(gap_sample, aes(x=infant_mortality, y=fertility)) +</code><br/><code>  geom_point(aes(color=continent)) +</code><br/><code>  geom_text(aes(label=country))</code></li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — a mapping in the ggplot() call applies to every layer. So geom_text also gets color=continent, and the country names are colored just like the points. To color only the points, put the color mapping in geom_point."><code>ggplot(gap_sample, aes(x=infant_mortality, y=fertility, color=continent)) +</code><br/><code>  geom_point() +</code><br/><code>  geom_text(aes(label=country))</code></li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — this is the other way around: the color mapping is only in geom_text, so the names are colored and the points are black. The label mapping in the ggplot() call is fine: geom_point simply ignores it."><code>ggplot(gap_sample, aes(x=infant_mortality, y=fertility, label=country)) +</code><br/><code>  geom_point() +</code><br/><code>  geom_text(aes(color=continent))</code></li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — outside aes(), color expects a constant like 'blue', not a column. R then looks for an object called continent outside the data, and gives the error: object 'continent' not found. To link color to a column, put it inside aes()."><code>ggplot(gap_sample, aes(x=infant_mortality, y=fertility)) +</code><br/><code>  geom_point(color=continent) +</code><br/><code>  geom_text(aes(label=country))</code></li>
</ul>
<p class="quiz-feedback" hidden></p>
</div>

<div class="quiz">
<div class="quiz-title">Q3: Not what I asked for</div>
<p class="quiz-question">Using <code>gap_2010</code>, which has the same columns as above but one row for every country, a student wants to make all points blue, and runs:</p>

<pre><code>ggplot(data=gap_2010, mapping=aes(x=infant_mortality, y=fertility)) +
  geom_point(aes(color="blue"))</code></pre>
<p>But the points turn out red, with a legend containing the single value "blue". What should they change?</p>
<ul class="quiz-choices">
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="true" data-explain="Right — inside aes(), ggplot treats 'blue' as a data value to map, just like a continent name: it becomes a single category, which gets the first color of the default palette (a reddish color). Outside aes(), color='blue' is a constant that simply makes every point blue.">Move the color outside <code>aes()</code>: <code>geom_point(color="blue")</code>.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — for points, color is the right aesthetic; fill is for the inside of areas such as bars. The problem is that the color is inside aes(), so ggplot treats 'blue' as a data value to map rather than as a color.">Use <code>fill="blue"</code> instead of <code>color="blue"</code>.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — without quotes, ggplot would look for a column called blue, and give an error because there isn't one. Blue is a literal value, so it needs quotes; it just shouldn't be inside aes().">Remove the quotes: <code>aes(color=blue)</code>.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — moving it to the ggplot() call would apply it to all layers, but it would still be a mapping inside aes(), with the same red points as a result. A constant color goes outside aes().">Move <code>color="blue"</code> into the <code>aes()</code> in the <code>ggplot()</code> call.</li>
</ul>
<p class="quiz-feedback" hidden></p>
</div>

<div class="quiz">
<div class="quiz-title">Q4: Decades as numbers</div>
<p class="quiz-question">These are some rows from <code>gdp_per_decade</code>, with the total GDP per continent per decade (shown here in trillions of dollars):</p>

| continent | decade | gdp |
|---|---:|---:|
| Asia | 1960 | 15.7 |
| Asia | 1970 | 30.8 |
| Asia | 1980 | 48.7 |
| Europe | 1960 | 22.2 |
| Europe | 1970 | 44.4 |
| Europe | 1980 | 59.5 |

<p>To compare the decades within each continent, the chapter uses:</p>

<pre><code>ggplot(gdp_per_decade, aes(x=continent, y=gdp, fill=as.factor(decade))) +
  geom_col(position="dodge")</code></pre>
<p>Why is the <code>as.factor</code> needed?</p>
<ul class="quiz-choices">
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="true" data-explain="Right — ggplot looks at the column type to decide what to do. A number gets a color gradient, and doesn't create groups, so the decades are drawn on top of each other in a single bar per continent. A factor is treated as a set of categories: one color and one bar per decade.">Because <code>decade</code> is a number, ggplot would use a color gradient instead of a separate bar and color for each decade.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — ggplot can map a numeric column to fill without any error: it then uses a color gradient, as it did for color=life_expectancy. The problem is that it then also doesn't make a separate bar per decade.">Without it, ggplot gives an error, because <code>fill</code> can only be used with text columns.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — as.factor only changes how the column is treated in the plot; it doesn't change the numbers. The years are still shown as 1960, 1970, and so on.">Otherwise the decades would be shown as 1.96, 1.97, and so on.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — as.factor changes how the decade column is treated (as categories rather than numbers). It doesn't change the gdp values or how they are summed.">Otherwise, <code>geom_col</code> would add up the GDP of all decades.</li>
</ul>
<p class="quiz-feedback" hidden></p>
</div>

<div class="quiz">
<div class="quiz-title">Q5: Dividing up the world</div>
<p class="quiz-question">Using the same <code>gdp_per_decade</code> data (one row per continent per decade), you now want a chart with one bar per decade, where the height of the bar shows the total world GDP, divided into colored parts for each continent. Which code does that?</p>
<ul class="quiz-choices">
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="true" data-explain="Right — with decade on the x axis you get one bar per decade, and mapping fill to continent splits each bar into a colored part per continent. By default, geom_col stacks these parts on top of each other, so the height of the bar is the world total."><code>ggplot(gdp_per_decade, aes(x=as.factor(decade), y=gdp, fill=continent)) +</code><br/><code>  geom_col()</code></li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — this is the grouped chart from the previous question: one group of bars per continent, with the decades next to each other. That compares decades within a continent, but it doesn't show the world total per decade."><code>ggplot(gdp_per_decade, aes(x=continent, y=gdp, fill=as.factor(decade))) +</code><br/><code>  geom_col(position="dodge")</code></li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — for bars, color is only the outline, while fill is the inside. This gives grey bars with a colored outline around each continent's part, which is very hard to read. Use fill for the inside of bars."><code>ggplot(gdp_per_decade, aes(x=as.factor(decade), y=gdp, color=continent)) +</code><br/><code>  geom_col()</code></li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — geom_bar doesn't use the gdp column at all: it counts the number of rows. Since there is one row per continent per decade, every bar would have a height of 5, with each continent counting as 1."><code>ggplot(gdp_per_decade, aes(x=as.factor(decade), fill=continent)) +</code><br/><code>  geom_bar()</code></li>
</ul>
<p class="quiz-feedback" hidden></p>
</div>

<div class="quiz">
<div class="quiz-title">Q6: Vertical lines everywhere</div>
<p class="quiz-question">These are the first rows of <code>gap</code>, which has one row for each country in each year:</p>

| country | year | continent | fertility |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| Albania | 1960 | Europe | 6.19 |
| Austria | 1960 | Europe | 2.70 |
| Belarus | 1960 | Europe | 2.74 |

<p>A student wants to show how fertility changed over time on each continent, and runs:</p>

<pre><code>ggplot(gap, aes(x=year, y=fertility, color=continent)) +
  geom_line()</code></pre>
<p>The result looks like this:</p>
<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="A line chart of fertility over time, colored by continent, in which each continent's line runs up and down vertically at every year and jumps diagonally to the next year" style="max-width: 100%;"/>
<p>What is going on?</p>
<ul class="quiz-choices">
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="true" data-explain="Right — ggplot draws one line per color, so all countries of a continent end up in the same line. For each year, that line goes up and down through all countries, and then jumps to the next year. The fix is to first compute a single value per continent and year (e.g. the mean fertility), or to add group=country to draw one line per country.">Each continent has many countries per year, and <code>geom_line</code> connects all of them into a single line per continent.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — ggplot already makes one group per continent, because continent is mapped to color. That is exactly the problem: all countries of a continent end up in the same line. You need either one value per continent and year, or group=country.">The lines need to be grouped per continent, so <code>group=continent</code> should be added to <code>aes()</code>.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — missing values would cause gaps in the lines, not vertical lines. The vertical lines appear because there are many rows (countries) for each year and continent, and they are all connected into one line.">Fertility has missing values, which causes the line to jump up and down.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — year is a number, which is exactly what you want on the x axis of a line chart. The problem is that there are many countries per year and continent, which are all connected into one line.">The year needs to be converted with <code>as.factor(year)</code>, so that each year is a separate category.</li>
</ul>
<p class="quiz-feedback" hidden></p>
</div>

<div class="quiz">
<div class="quiz-title">Q7: What happened in 1970?</div>
<p class="quiz-question">These are the rows for Asia in <code>below_replacement</code>, which counts the countries with a fertility below 2.1 per continent and year. It was made with <code>filter(fertility &lt; 2.1)</code>, followed by <code>group_by(year, continent)</code> and <code>summarize(n = n())</code>:</p>

| year | continent | n |
|---:|---|---:|
| 1968 | Asia | 1 |
| 1969 | Asia | 1 |
| 1971 | Asia | 1 |
| 1972 | Asia | 1 |

<p>In 1970, no Asian country had a fertility below 2.1. What does the Asia line in <code>ggplot(below_replacement) + geom_line(aes(x=year, y=n, color=continent))</code> show for 1970?</p>
<ul class="quiz-choices">
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="true" data-explain="Right — because no Asian country passed the filter in 1970, there is no row for it at all. ggplot simply connects 1969 to 1971 with a straight line, so the plot suggests there was 1 country, while the real number was 0. Using complete(year, continent, fill=list(n=0)) adds the missing row with n = 0.">1, because ggplot draws a straight line from 1969 to 1971.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — that would be the correct value, but there is no row for Asia in 1970 in the data. ggplot can't know that a missing row means zero; it just connects the points it has. To get the zero, add it with complete(year, continent, fill=list(n=0)).">0, because no Asian country had a fertility below 2.1 in that year.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — a gap appears when a row exists with an NA value. Here, the row is missing entirely, so ggplot just connects 1969 to 1971 with a straight line.">Nothing: the line has a gap at 1970.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — ggplot doesn't need a row for every year: it just connects the points that are there, without any warning. That is what makes this gotcha easy to miss.">The plot gives an error, because the year 1970 is missing.</li>
</ul>
<p class="quiz-feedback" hidden></p>
</div>
